cards.text: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus, is writing to the saints in Ephesus, and he's a prisoner (Eph 1:1; 3:1). Back in verse 1 he started a sentence, then took a twelve-verse detour to explain a mystery: through the gospel, the Gentiles are fellow heirs (Eph 3:1-6). Now he finally picks that sentence back up, and friend, I RESPECT a man who comes back for his sentence.

cards.question: Paul finally gets back to his sentence, and he comes before the Father. How does he do it?

cards.text: Paul calls Him the Father from whom every family in heaven and on earth derives its name. Friend, I asked an angel for exactly ONE thing, to keep my name, so this line gets me right in the apron.
Now remember, Paul's a prisoner, and he calls his sufferings for these people their glory (Eph 3:1, 13). Me? I'd be praying about my own situation. Paul prays for THEM.

cards.question: Paul is praying for the saints in Ephesus. What's the first thing he asks the Father to do for them?
Paul asks the Father to strengthen these believers. Where does Paul say that strength comes out of?
Paul is praying for these believers to get stronger on the outside, where everyone can see it.
Paul asks God to strengthen them with power through His ___ in their inner being.
Paul wants that inner strength for them so Christ may dwell in their hearts through faith.

cards.text: Then Paul paints a picture with two words: these believers are rooted and grounded in love. Roots like a tree, ground like a building, and the thing underneath it all is love.

cards.question: Paul pictures these believers rooted and grounded in love. What does that picture say about love for them?

answers.text: It's what they stand on and grow from
It's a feeling that comes and goes
It's a reward they earn by trying

cards.text: Paul isn't done praying. He says these believers will have power to grasp something BIG.

cards.question: Paul says these believers in Ephesus will have power to grasp something big, and he pictures each of them grasping it all alone.
Paul says they'll comprehend the length and width and height and depth of something. What is it?
Paul wants them to know the love of Christ, a love that surpasses knowledge. What does he mean?

answers.text: It's bigger than our minds can hold
It's only for the very wise
It fades once you learn it

cards.text: Then Paul prays they'd be filled with all the fullness of God. Friend, I fill cookie boxes for a LIVING, and if I ever tried to fit ALL of anything into one, that box would need to go lie down somewhere.

cards.question: Paul turns from asking to praising. Compared to all we ask or imagine, how much is God able to do?
Paul says God is able to do immeasurably more, according to His power that is at work ___ us.
Paul closes with "to Him be the glory in the church and in Christ Jesus," and he means only for his own generation.

cards.text: Forever and ever, and Paul seals it with one word: Amen. A prisoner just prayed the biggest prayer I've ever heard, and friend, I've got goosebumps under this apron.

findings.problem: This non-opening story card exceeds the two-sentence limit. After the background sentence, it uses both the 'Me? I'd be praying...' exchange and 'Paul prays for THEM.', making at least three sentence units even before counting 'Me?' separately.

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: Cards 2 and 5 already use discovery questions. Cards 7-9 then require unrevealed details: that the strength is inward rather than outward, that it comes through the Spirit, and that its purpose is Christ dwelling in their hearts through faith. The earlier cards give no basis for reasoning out those picks, so most of this stop's choices become discovery or luck rather than informed guesses.

rule.text: Before each choice card, Papa Dorin's story card gives enough context that the baker can reason their way to the answer. A few of those are okay, as long as most choice cards are informed guesses.

findings.problem: The blank asks for the exact BSB word 'Spirit' in wording the baker has not yet seen. No earlier card introduces the Spirit or gives a textual basis for eliminating Law and Sabbath, so this is completing an unseen line rather than reasoning out its meaning.

rule.text: The blank tests meaning the baker can reason out, not wording they haven't seen.

findings.problem: The right answer itself, 'The love of Christ,' comes from Ephesians 3:19. Verse 18 supplies the setup about the dimensions, so the choice-card citation is wider than the verse of its right answer; it should cite Ephesians 3:19.

rule.text: A choice card cites only the verses of its right answer.
